title: The Cavity Detective
briefing: Ethan, 14, keeps a bottle of sweet iced tea on his desk and sips it all afternoon. At his checkup, the dentist finds two soft, chalky spots starting on his back teeth. His sister drinks the same tea every day too — and her teeth are fine.
question: Same drink, same sugar — why are Ethan's teeth losing and his sister's aren't?

clues.title: All-afternoon sipper
clues.text: Ethan takes a sip of sweet iced tea every few minutes from 2 p.m. to 6 p.m. The bottle lasts all afternoon.
clues.shows: sugar arriving in his mouth again and again all afternoon

clues.title: Soft spots
clues.text: At his checkup, two spots on his back teeth are chalky and soft — the start of cavities.
clues.shows: the hard enamel surface being dissolved over time

clues.title: Same drink, one go
clues.text: His sister drinks the same bottle of the same tea, but all of it with lunch. They both brush twice a day with the same toothpaste.
clues.shows: the same sugar doing far less harm when it all comes at once

clues.title: Twenty minutes each time
clues.text: A test strip shows Ethan's mouth turns acidic within a minute of each sip. It takes about twenty minutes to get back to normal.
clues.shows: each sip starting about twenty minutes of acid

visual.unit: minutes of acid per afternoon, sister → Ethan

hypotheses.text: He drinks more sugar than his sister.
hypotheses.flaw: They drink the same amount of the same tea — the only difference is how it's spread through the day.
He brushes twice a day with the same toothpaste as his sister.

hypotheses.text: Bacteria in his mouth turn sugar into acid, and every sip starts about twenty minutes of acid softening his enamel. Sipping every few minutes means the acid never stops, so his saliva never gets the chance to repair the enamel.
Iced tea is too cold for teeth.
hypotheses.flaw: His sister drinks the same cold tea with no damage — and coldness doesn't dissolve enamel.

prediction.prompt: Ethan drinks the same amount of sweet tea each day but splits it into more and more separate sips — from none up to twenty. What happens to the minutes of acid attack on his teeth each day?

second.question: If he brushed more often, what would happen to the acid minutes?

concepts.label: mouth bacteria
concepts.hint: What living things in his mouth feed on the sugar?

concepts.label: sugar becomes acid
concepts.hint: What do those bacteria make from sugar?

concepts.label: acid softens enamel
concepts.hint: What does the acid do to the outside of the tooth?

concepts.label: how often, not how much
concepts.hint: What was different about the way Ethan drank?

concepts.label: saliva repairs between sips
concepts.hint: What fixes the enamel when the acid stops — and why did it never get its turn?

transfer.context: Nia chews sugary gum, one piece after another, from the start of school until lunch. Her brother eats the same amount of sugar as one dessert after dinner. Who is more likely to get soft spots on their teeth?
options: Her brother, because dessert has more sugar.
Both the same, because the sugar is the same.
Nia, because each piece keeps acid attacking her teeth all morning, with no break for saliva to repair them.
transfer.retryHint: Same amount of sugar, different timing — which of Ethan's clues compared him with his sister?
transfer.explanation: The sugar is the same, but Nia feeds her mouth bacteria again and again all morning, so the acid never stops. Her brother's dessert causes one twenty-minute acid attack, and then his saliva gets hours to repair the enamel — just like Ethan's sister drinking her tea with lunch.

takeaway: Teeth care about how often, not just how much. Every sugary sip feeds mouth bacteria that make acid for about twenty minutes; spread the sips all day and the acid never stops, so saliva never gets its turn to repair the enamel.
